newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Bridas hopes its Turkmen oil/gas setback temporary.
newsitem.headline: Bridas hopes its Turkmen oil/gas setback temporary.

text.p: Argentinian oil and gas independent Bridas Energy Corp hopes to be a big player in Turkmenistan despite setbacks for one of the first energy investors in the Central Asian state, a Bridas adviser said.
"We see these problems as a glitch in our relationship with the Turkmen government rather than a break," Malcolm Hurlston of MHCC Ltd, advisors to Bridas, said on Thursday.
He was speaking at an international energy conference in the Turkmen capital Ashgabat.

Bridas is pursuing two separate legal actions related to its Turkmen projects -- one against Turkmenistan in the international arbitration courts and one against Unocal Corp of the United States in a U.S. court.
Hurlston said potential investors in Turkmenistan's huge untapped oil and gas reserves were following the cases closely, adding, "people are closely watching what happens to Bridas."

Bridas is suing Unocal for what it called "tortuous interference" in a plan Bridas developed to export Yashlar gas to Pakistan via Afghanistan. It expects court hearings in Fort Bend county, near Houston, to start in November.

Bridas set up a joint-venture with Turkmenistan in 1992 to develop the huge Yashlar gas field in eastern Turkmenistan, which has estimated reserves of 27 trillion cubic feet and 165 million barrels of liquid hydrocarbons.
It said it put forward plans to export the gas to Pakistan via Afghanistan and that it proposed to the Turkmen government to set up a consortium to build the pipeline.

But Turkmenistan granted Unocal rights in October 1995 to set up a consortium to build a pipeline from the Turkmen-Afghan border to Multan in northern Pakistan and market Turkmen gas from the huge Dauletabad field, in production since 1983.
The project would be in direct competition to Bridas'.

At an oil and gas conference this week, Unocal representatives shared the rostrum with senior Turkmenistan energy officials, who said they had selected Unocal as consortium leader, a decision since confirmed by Pakistan.
Unocal International Energy Ventures Marty Miller said the company did not want to comment on the case at this stage.

Unocal's proposal envisages constructing a gas pipeline from the Turkmen-Afghan border to Multan in northern Pakistan via Afghanistan at an estimated cost of $1.9 billion, with an extension to northern India at a cost of $600 million.
Bridas' second action concerns another joint-venture with Turkmenistan in 1993 to develop the Keimir oil field.
Hurlston said Turkmenistan had asked for changes to the original contract on more than one occasion, blocking Bridas from exporting oil while talks were held.
Output at the field was stopped in 1996 once storage was full. It was producing 17,000 barrels per day (bpd) at its peak. Total Turkmenistan oil output last year was 110,000 bpd.
Hurlston said international arbitration hearings were due to start in June or July.

In a further twist to the tale, Bridas won a deal last month to upgrade Kazakhstan's gas pipeline system, which forms part of the former Soviet network and carries Turkmen gas to Russia's export routes and on to Western Europe.
Energy sources at the conference said the deal was unpopular with Turkmenistan, which relies entirely on the pipeline network to move its gas to hard-currency markets.
But Hurlston played down any risk to Turkmen supplies.
"I can see that they might be concerned, but they needn't be worried," he said. "It is not our pipeline."
He added that Turkmenistan remained a country of huge potential for foreign oil and gas investments.
"If these problems can be resolved, this could be a great country to invest in," he said.
